blogs.title: When Computers 'Receive': Statutory Interpretation in the Age of Automation
blogs.description: This post will analyze the Fifth Circuit's holding that GoAuto's automated computer system receiving an email satisfied the statutory 'receipt' requirement. The court's pragmatic reasoning—that 'company computers do much that individuals once did'—represents a significant statement on how courts should interpret statutory terms in light of modern business practices. The post will examine the implications for other statutes requiring 'receipt,' 'delivery,' or 'notice,' and discuss whether courts should analogize automated processes to human actions or develop new interpretive frameworks for digital-age statutory construction.

blogs.title: Strict Adherence or Strict Construction? The Paradox of Louisiana's Insurance Cancellation Doctrine
blogs.description: This post will explore the doctrinal tension at the heart of the court's analysis: Louisiana law demands 'strict adherence' to statutory cancellation procedures, yet the court refused to read a signature requirement into the statute. The plaintiffs argued that strict adherence meant capturing every conceivable procedural protection, while the court held that strict adherence means following what is written—no more and no less. The post will examine what this tension reveals about consumer protection in insurance contexts and whether 'strict adherence' doctrines invite purposive or textualist interpretation.

blogs.title: Certification Reluctance and the Fifth Circuit's Erie Guesses
blogs.description: This post will focus on the Fifth Circuit's declination to certify the statutory interpretation questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court despite acknowledging the absence of controlling state authority on signature and receipt requirements. The court invoked its general reluctance to 'go to that well too often,' but this case involves significant questions affecting Louisiana's insurance industry. The post will situate this decision within broader debates about federal courts' certification practices, the Erie doctrine, and whether federal courts making predictive interpretations of state law serves federalism values or undermines state law development.
